summary.text: 打 combines 扌, the side form of 手 ‘hand,’ with 丁 as a sound component. Its received Shuowen New Attached analysis glosses it as ‘strike’; a curated seal-script-style redraw shows the same pairing. The graph is also used for Mandarin dá ‘a dozen,’ a separate word associated with English dozen.

formation.text: Phonosemantic: 手, written in its conventional left-side form 扌, contributes the hand/action category; 丁 supplies a phonetic cue. The New Attached Shuowen analysis supports this construction and the gloss ‘strike.’

components.text: 扌 is the conventional left-side form of 手 ‘hand.’ In 打 it contributes the hand/action category; the seal-style redraw depicts it beside 丁. It is a positional form, not evidence of a chronological replacement.

丁 is the right-hand phonetic component in the received analysis. Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions give 丁 *rteːŋ/*teːŋ and 打 *rteŋʔ/*teːŋʔ, sharing an onset, rhyme, and nasal; these reconstructions support a sound relationship but do not record ancient speech directly.

sound_limitation.text: The cited sound comparison is reconstructed and system-dependent; it does not establish the precise historical relation or provide a direct recording of either pronunciation.

sound.text: The reported Old Chinese forms share onset, rhyme, and nasal; the reconstructions differ in details, so the comparison supports the phonetic role without fixing its exact history.

history.text: The received Shuowen lacks 打 in its main text; the graph appears in the Song-era New Attached section, where it is analyzed as hand plus phonetic 丁. A curated seal-script-style image is a modern redraw associated with that tradition, not a dated artifact or proof of a sequence of graphic changes.

The consulted character database lists a small-seal form but no oracle-bone or bronze examples. This absence from the consulted listings does not show that the graph could not have existed earlier. A proposed connection to forms written with 木, including possible confusion or replacement, remains unestablished; no particular corruption path is supported.

uncertainties.text: The earliest attestation is unsettled. A Han-period poem is cited with 打 meaning ‘strike,’ and scholarship discusses earlier dictionary citations and a gloss roughly meaning ‘to knock or strike out’; the witnesses and transmission do not securely establish an earlier Shuowen text or settle the dating.

The older nasal reading and modern dǎ have a documented reading history, but explanations for the later open-rime form compete, including analogy and regional loss of the nasal ending. The evidence does not establish one path.

A proposed comparison of the striking word with Mizo dêng and Proto-Mon-Khmer *dah/*daʔ remains tentative: sound correspondences, chronology, cognacy, and borrowing direction are unresolved in this evidence.

senses.text: A Han-period poem cited by a character database uses 打 for striking. Early dictionary citations and a gloss roughly meaning ‘to knock or strike out’ are also discussed, but their transmission leaves the earliest attestation unsettled.

senses.period: Examples cited from the Liang period and later
senses.text: Later dated examples document uses for attacking and fighting. The evidence establishes these uses, not a direct semantic path from one to the other or from a particular earlier sense.
A Song-period example records a use meaning ‘make’ or ‘manufacture’; its connection and path from the striking sense are not established here.
A Song example records ‘take/catch fish.’ The evidence does not establish when or how this sense developed from other uses.
A Tang example documents a prepositional use marking place, direction, or time. Its semantic development is not demonstrated by the cited example.

senses.gloss: a dozen; a unit of twelve
senses.text: Mandarin dá is a separate word for a dozen, associated with English dozen and the reported spelling 打臣. The graph was reused to write this word; the account proposes an English-derived spelling, not a semantic development from ‘strike.’ The dossier does not date its first Chinese attestation or establish the intermediate form’s chronology.

developments.text: Attack and fighting uses are documented later than the cited Han-period striking use, but the examples do not prove a direct development from that sense.

limitations.text: Separate period examples document striking, attacking or fighting, making, catching fish, and a prepositional use, but do not establish their full chronology or direct semantic connections.
The dozen use is associated with English dozen, but this evidence does not establish its first Chinese attestation or a dated intermediate form.

overview.text: 打 pairs the hand form 扌 with 丁 as a sound component to write ‘strike.’ The same graph also writes dá ‘a dozen,’ a separate word associated with English dozen.

components.text: 扌 is the side form of 手 ‘hand’; here it marks the hand/action category.
丁 supplies a sound cue. The cited comparison is reconstructed, not a direct recording of ancient speech.

takeaway.text: The dozen sense is a borrowed use of the whole graph for another word, not a meaning shown to grow from ‘strike.’

relationships.text: In 打, 扌 is the side form of 手 and contributes the hand/action category.
The received analysis assigns 丁 the phonetic role in 打; reported Old Chinese reconstructions support a sound comparison.
